name: chafa
desc: Versatile and fast Unicode/ASCII/ANSI graphics renderer
why: Renders images as terminal art, turning pixels into Unicode and ANSI with surprisingly good fidelity.

brief.what_it_is: Chafa is a command-line utility, with a C library behind it, that converts image data into terminal graphics. It takes in common image formats, including animated GIFs, and writes out ANSI/Unicode character art or terminal graphics protocols such as Sixels, Kitty and iTerm2. Its default output mixes several Unicode symbol ranges, and it can also be used as a library through a documented C API, with Python and JavaScript bindings maintained by others.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches it as a way to view reasonable approximations of pictures and animations in a terminal emulator. It notes that other terminal graphics tools use only U+2580 (upper half block), and says Chafa's wider symbol set gives much better quality by default.
brief.how_it_works: Chafa maps image pixels onto a selectable set of Unicode symbols and colours, using Truecolor, 256-colour, 16-colour or FG/BG modes. Glyphs can be loaded from any FreeType-supported font file, and it can measure colour in RGB or DIN99d space. The homepage describes it as SIMD-optimised and multithreaded.

commands_seen.context: Restricts output to the upper half block (U+2580) only, to show the simpler rendering the homepage compares against.

brief.install_notes: Most distributions package Chafa, and the README recommends official packages unless you want to hack on it. To build from git you need GCC, make, Autoconf, Automake, Libtool and GLib development packages. For the chafa command-line tool you also need FreeType2. Optional dev packages add support for AVIF, libdeflate (faster PNG), HEIF 1.12+, JPEG, JPEG XL, librsvg, TIFF and WebP. gtk-doc is needed only to build documentation. No accounts or runtime configuration are mentioned.
brief.standout: Rather than a single block-character fallback, it combines Unicode symbols from several selectable ranges and can draw glyphs from real font files, while also emitting pixel-accurate protocols like Sixels and Kitty. The homepage ships its own blog series with a sense of humour.
brief.status: Appears actively maintained, but the evidence is indirect. The homepage's newest blog post is 'Chafa 1.14', the README has a live release badge and build-status badge but no dated release or commit in the text I read, and I did not check the GitHub commit history or the download page.
brief.caveats: Output is approximate by nature: the homepage calls it 'very, very reasonable approximations'. Building from source needs several C libraries, and most of the image-format support depends on optional dependencies. Licence is LGPLv3 or later. The Matrix chat is the stated support channel and its history is hidden from non-members.
